## [2026-10-28](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-28.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645>)

MERLIN stores compact first and second moments of each segment’s keys and uses query-dependent alignment means and variances to combine recurrent-memory readouts. Mid-training improves long-context retrieval in two small recurrent backbones, offering a more informative alternative to routing from mean keys alone while retaining an explicit memory-quality trade-off.

**Published:** 2026-10-27 · **First seen:** 2026-10-28T10:02:23.982Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Recurrent Memory, Linear Attention, Moment Routing, Long Context

**Public availability:** 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/new?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.37645v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete 20-page v1 inspected. Uniform 256-token segments and RULER-style augmented mid-training convert Gated DeltaNet-1.3B/Mamba-2-780M to multi-state models. At 16K, LongBench averages reach 21.9/20.6 versus mean-routing 19.3/18.4; RULER averages 62.7/76.2 versus 57.9/71.2. These are benchmark scores, not percentage-point gains from the abstract’s relative percentages. Original October 28 cs.CL new listing and official Tuesday schedule imply 00:00 UTC announcement. No author implementation destination was verified.

**Limitations:** One recorded seed and two backbones at 16K; some individual tasks regress. The state bank grows with segment count, and second-moment storage adds overhead; no measured serving speedup is established. The softmax connection motivates rather than exactly reproduces attention. Main text adds 60M second-stage tokens while appendix summarizes 2B, leaving budget accounting imperfect.

## [2026-10-27](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-27.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [LoopFold: Parallelizing Recurrent Depth in Looped Transformers](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35556>)

LoopFold predicts inputs to later recurrent layers so several depths of a shared Transformer can run in parallel, then corrects their outputs using newly available earlier states. Joint training turns extra parallel computation into a shorter sequential decoding path, offering a useful architecture tradeoff between latency, quality and memory.

**Published:** 2026-10-26 · **First seen:** 2026-10-27T10:06:55.058Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Looped Transformers, Parallel Recurrent Depth, Architecture, Compute-Memory Tradeoffs

**Public availability:** 2026-10-27T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.35556v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete 13-page v1 inspected. Models train from scratch on 30B Pile tokens at 1.4B scale. At target depth 9, five stages use 21 backbone evaluations versus nine sequential evaluations, with 46% lower batch-one decoding latency and eight-task accuracy 56.38% versus 54.18%. Separate matched-backbone-compute comparisons show smaller quality gains. Original Tuesday batch and official schedule imply October 27 00:00UTC announcement.

**Limitations:** Schedules train separately; this is not exact trajectory-preserving parallelization of an existing checkpoint. Extra FLOPs and KV caches are material costs. Timings use 1024-token prompts/continuations, BF16, no tensor parallelism and an unspecified GPU model. No multi-seed uncertainty or author implementation destination was verified.

## [2026-10-22](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-22.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Loopholing All the Way: Language Modeling with pure Self-Conditioning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30068>)

LAW repeatedly refines continuous expected token embeddings and samples discrete tokens only at the end, making self-conditioning the complete generative state rather than an auxiliary hint. Matched-training-compute experiments improve constraint solving and small-scale mathematical reasoning, suggesting an alternative to interleaving discrete token resampling with denoising. The evidence does not yet establish frontier-scale quality or wall-clock speedups.

**Published:** 2026-10-21 · **First seen:** 2026-10-22T10:05:15.328Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Diffusion Language Models, Self-conditioning, Continuous Generation

**Public availability:** 2026-10-22T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30068v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Pinned v1 Sections 3–5 and relevant task, compute, training and generation appendices inspected. LAW initializes token embeddings from uniformly sampled tokens, feeds a noncausal denoiser only the continuous self-conditioning state, and updates that state with the probability-weighted expected token embedding. Prompt positions remain fixed clean embeddings, and a categorical token projection is deferred to the end. Training still uses a discrete-diffusion-corrupted initialization and task-specific cross-entropy or negative-ELBO objectives; pure self-conditioning describes sampling, not absence of a diffusion-derived training objective. Default training uses two passes with probability 0.9, stop-gradient between passes and loss only on the final pass, with randomized self-conditioning temperature; OpenWebText also uses a learned mode embedding. Estimated training FLOPs count a backward pass as twice a forward pass, so these settings cost 3.9 forward-pass equivalents per update versus 3 for the comparison, and LAW uses about 77% as many steps. Academic 8-layer and 12-layer DiT experiments cover Sudoku, mazes, TinyGSM-to-GSM8K and OpenWebText. The reported hard Sudoku score is 96.5% versus 91.0% for the retrained LDDM-U comparison at 180 function evaluations. The matched-FLOP 12-layer TinyGSM study reports 42.2% GSM8K accuracy versus 34.5% for LDDM-U at temperature 1 and 1,024 function evaluations. The Maze metric accepts any valid shortest path, rather than reference-path exact match. OpenWebText evidence uses external-model generative perplexity alongside unigram entropy, with a quality/diversity tradeoff as iterations increase; it is not a measured wall-clock speed comparison. The original October 21 receipt (17:25:08 UTC) is retained. The original October 22 new-submission batch and official Eastern-time schedule imply October 22 00:00 UTC availability; no earlier primary artifact was verified in the bounded search. The paper-announced author code URL and GitHub API both return 404, so no available-code link is claimed.

**Limitations:** The tested models and contexts are small academic setups, with task-specific objectives and tuned sampling settings; no frontier-scale language or chat capability result is established. Matched estimated training FLOPs do not mean matched wall-clock time, and numbers of function evaluations are not end-to-end latency. The paper mixes retrained comparisons and prior reported puzzle results, so the evidence should not be generalized into universal benchmark leadership. Main reported results do not provide a broad multi-training-seed uncertainty study. OpenWebText external-model perplexity and unigram entropy are incomplete quality/diversity proxies. Training still uses diffusion corruption and, for some tasks, a diffusion-derived bound. The announced author repository was unavailable (404), limiting artifact verification. No independent reproduction.

### [MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26825>)

MemT-1.0 adds trainable memory modules to frozen language-model backbones with stable token-level state updates, and studies densely routed memory experts as a way to expand capacity. Its released models turn growing interaction histories into bounded persistent states, offering predictable session storage while exposing a clear trade-off between compact memory and precise historical recall.

**Published:** 2026-10-19 · **First seen:** 2026-10-21T10:08:20.059Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Native Memory, Recurrent State, Mixture of Storage, Continued Pretraining

**Public availability:** 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.26825v1>) · [Code](<https://github.com/MemTensor/MemT-1.0>) · [Project](<https://huggingface.co/collections/MemTensor/memt-1>)

**Evidence:** technical-report; full-text. Pinned v1 architecture/training Sections2–3, memory evaluation Section6, limitations Section8 and relevant configuration/evaluation appendices inspected. Gated DeltaNet-2 writes token-level information at turn/segment boundaries, while generation reads the incoming state. The explored Mixture-of-Storage expansion routes densely across all memory experts, not sparse top-k experts; both released Nano and Flash configurations use one memory expert per selected layer (Appendix B, Table6), while expanded MoS is studied separately. The34B-token pipeline uses current-segment CE followed by off-policy full-context-teacher distillation with Top64 forward-KL targets. Only memory parameters are optimized during native-memory training. Nano uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and451M trainable memory parameters; Flash uses a separately prepared DeepSeek-V4-Flash backbone and3.61B memory parameters. Across11 memory benchmarks their reported macro-averages are47.0 and50.6, ahead of tested parametric-memory baselines but below strong textual-memory methods. At128K history, Nano reports1.86x end-to-end inference speed and66x less logical per-trajectory state than full-context KV. The speed test uses HF inference on two GPUs, batch/concurrency1,35 histories, a fixed512-token query and forced128-token response, including history preparation/state restoration but excluding loading/tokenization/scoring. The original CL October20 batch/schedule gives an inferred October20T00Z paper announcement; the observed release commit (authored October20T02:48:07Z, committed05:27:44Z) contains code and a complete tech\_report.pdf. These Git timestamps document content history, not exact first public visibility. Code/project links were verified, not executed.

**Limitations:** Fixed state cannot retain unlimited detail: exact recall deteriorates and retrieval/text-memory systems remain stronger on aggregate. The66x figure excludes shared backbone weights, embedders/hyper-memory parameters and is logical persistent session state, not total GPU-memory savings. The1.86x speedup is one specific HF workload and is mainly history-preparation savings; short histories are slower, and heterogeneous baseline backbones/runtimes limit broad efficiency rankings. Dense expert expansion increases memory computation. General-capability preservation is evaluated under specified noise conditions, not a guarantee of unchanged behavior. Application-specific experience training/retrieval adds costs; online state updates are not autonomous weight-level self-improvement. The October20v2 revision is not used for this report’s cutoff.

## [2026-10-15](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-15.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20456>)

COUNT adds corpus-count memory during language-model pretraining by combining the model's output embeddings using read-only n-gram statistics stored in host RAM. Models trained with COUNT can later adapt by swapping these tables without updating their weights, providing a way to improve language modeling and domain specialization through additional host memory.

**Published:** 2026-10-14 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T15:10:36.803Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** N-gram Memory, Pretraining, Host Memory, Domain Adaptation

**Public availability:** 2026-10-15T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20456>) · [Code](<https://github.com/IanMagnusson/COUNT>) · [Project](<https://huggingface.co/datasets/IanMagnusson/count-ngram-tables>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. October 15 public availability is inferred from the dated new-submission batch and official schedule. Sections 2–6 and Appendix A inspect 60M–1B backbones, 11 validation sources and 74 downstream configurations; fitted loss frontiers correspond to 46–89% more standard-transformer 6ND compute. Author code, tables and checkpoints are accessible.

**Limitations:** Flagship tables require about 797 GB host RAM and summarize the full Dolma corpus; table construction and extra gather work are outside 6ND. Measured throughput is slightly lower, not faster. COUNT requires modified pretraining; domain accuracy gains are mixed, and released core code omits the optimized runtime used for throughput measurements. No independent reproduction.

### [Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14423>)

This work fits multimodal pretraining laws that account for directional transfer, competition for model capacity and diminishing returns from repeated vision or audio data. Controlled mixture-of-experts experiments make the framework useful for planning how to divide a training budget among model size, unique data and modality mixtures, while requiring coefficients to be fitted for the intended setup.

### [Overcoming Data Imbalances with Expert Selection Biases](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13370>)

COAX adds category-dependent biases to expert selection during pretraining, giving scarce languages or modalities a larger preferred expert pool while keeping the number of active experts per token fixed. This supplies a simple capacity-allocation control for imbalanced training mixtures, with most multilingual and multimodal loss gains retained after removing the bias for standard inference.

Kimi K3 combines hybrid recurrent and latent attention, attention across residual layers, and a sparse expert architecture in a native multimodal model with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 104 billion activated parameters. Its public report connects architecture, data, optimization, and long-context post-training, providing a current reference for how several efficiency improvements support scaling a large open-weight model.
